title: Login, domain and area code
prompt: The IT team sets up accounts from the HR table. Write `solve(employees)` so it returns `employee_id`, `login`, `domain` and `area_code`.
rules: Standardize `email` first: no spaces at the start or end, all lower case. `login` is the part before the `@` and `domain` the part after it.
An email without an `@` has no domain (missing), and its login is the whole standardized email. The job must not stop.
`area_code` is the first three of the phone's last ten digits, ignoring dashes, dots, spaces, brackets and a leading `+1`.
Missing values give missing results. Return the four columns, in that order, one row per employee.
hints: `F.split(email, "@")` makes a list of the parts. Build it from the trimmed, lower-case email.
`.getItem(1)` stops the job when there's no second part. `F.get(parts, 1)` gives `NULL` instead.
For the phone: keep the digits with `regexp_replace`, take the last ten with `F.substring(digits, -10, 10)`, then the first three of those.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(employees):
    # Return employee_id, login, domain and area_code.
    return employees
explanation: Standardize, split, and read the parts safely. `email = F.lower(F.trim("email"))` and `parts = F.split(email, "@")`; then `F.get(parts, 0)` is the login and `F.get(parts, 1)` the domain. With no `@` the list has one part, so `get` gives `NULL` for the domain, where `getItem(1)` would stop the job. Lower-casing before the split matters: `Ines.novak@Corp.Example` must give the domain `corp.example`. For the area code, `digits = F.regexp_replace("phone", "[^0-9]", "")`, then `F.substring(F.substring(digits, -10, 10), 1, 3)`: taking the first three digits straight from `digits` would give `155` for a number written with `+1`.
